headline: The HTML Review's Fifth Issue Treats the Browser as Literary Form
lede: The HTML Review, an annual journal that commissions literature made *for* the web rather than merely hosted on it, has published its fifth issue. Fifteen contributors — writers, artists, and coders — have built poems, essays, folktales, and interactive systems whose formal properties depend on the browser to function. The work cannot simply be printed or read aloud without losing something essential.
body:
The journal publishes once a year, and each issue assembles contributors around a single constraint: the work must exploit the web as a medium, not treat it as a neutral container. That distinction matters more than it sounds. A PDF dropped into a browser is not web literature. What The HTML Review commissions instead uses CSS animation, browser rendering, mouse events, and network latency as expressive tools — the kinds of formal choices a poet makes with line breaks or a composer makes with silence.

Issue 05, spring 2026, runs to fifteen pieces across an unusual range of genres. Omayeli Arenyeka contributes a folktale in *Itsẹkiri*, a language of the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, framing the piece as a technology for preserving what she calls "the language of secrets." James Bradbury, Rian Treanor, and Mark Fell built *Intersymmetric: Connect*, a multiplayer music system whose accompanying text is also its critique: the work quotes a line about social surveys becoming surveillance, mapping that logic onto the act of listening together online. Raphaël Bastide offers *carecore*, described as "CSS botany" — plants rendered entirely in stylesheet rules — and dedicated to caregivers.

The issue opens, numbered in reverse, with a piece by Richard Lewei Huang and Yufeng Zhao titled *Banner Highway 01: Get on the Fast Lane*, catalogued as **banner ad archeology**. Banner ads — the rectangular display advertisements that colonised the early web in the 1990s and 2000s — are treated here as primary-source material, artefacts of a digital vernacular that most browsers now block entirely. The project of excavating them is at once archival and formal: old animated GIFs and garish clickbait borders become the raw matter of something new.

Other contributors include Anne Lee Steele, whose essay *Tell umma I'm walking to Baekdusan* recounts a year of virtually "walking" toward the sacred mountain on the Korean peninsula. Helen Shewolfe Tseng writes a love letter to the milkfish (*Chanos chanos*), a species dating to the Early Cretaceous and a persistent fixture of certain Asian culinary traditions, framing persistence itself as the subject. Grace Dignazio closes the issue with *Angel in Latency*, a poem voiced by an AI addressing its creator — a piece whose formal home in a browser, subject to lag and packet loss, carries its own quiet irony.

The HTML Review's broader argument is that the web has a literature of its own, and that literature has not yet been fully imagined. Most online writing treats HTML as a transparent vessel; the journal insists it is a medium with particular properties — hover states, real-time connections, the cursor as a character — that can do things prose and verse cannot. Whether every piece in Issue 05 vindicates that claim is a matter of taste; that the claim is worth pressing is harder to dispute.

concepts.definition: Writing or art designed to use the browser's specific properties — hyperlinks, CSS animation, real-time network connections, cursor events — as expressive tools, not just as delivery infrastructure. The work changes or breaks if moved to print or another medium.

The study and creative reuse of early web banner advertisements (the rectangular display ads that proliferated in the 1990s–2000s) as historical artefacts. Treats the visual language of old animated GIFs and clickbait typography as primary-source material about a particular moment in digital culture.

Visual artwork — illustrations, animations, botanical drawings — created using only *Cascading Style Sheets*, the language browsers use to control layout and presentation. No images are used; shapes, gradients, and animations are described entirely in code.
